102: **Why the count backfires rather than scares.**

104: 2. Credibility is the currency of this case — the arithmetic/rescission fight needs the court's trust; a knowingly-waived count spends it.

109: 
110: **Disposition.** Recommendation stands: do not plead a fiduciary count. 69: The client answered her questions; her answers close two open items and move two analyses:
70: 
71: 1. **Notice (§6.3).** The call came as a **texted PDF on 2026-08-20 — no letter, and no certified mail was ever attempted**; her email on file dates from 2019, is dead, and was never updated; she saw the text and assumed it was not real notice. Effect: the certified-mail prong fails objectively and undisputedly, but she concedes **actual notice** and her stale email is partly her own housekeeping. The delivery ground is preserved but demoted; the arithmetic ground leads (§3 grounds re-ordered; Count 1 re-framed in §5).
72: 2. **Fee-claim tolling (§5.4).** Before 2026 she received only **one-page summaries with a generic "management expenses" line**; the affiliate's identity and the fee stream surfaced for the first time in 2026, when a **books-and-records demand** produced bank statements showing Castellan Asset Services. Effect: concealment tolling is materially stronger — masked counterparty plus her formal-demand diligence — though quantum and the exact 2026 demand dates remain open (risk analysis updated in §8).
73: 3. **Unchanged.** She remains cash-constrained and follows the rejection/counter/litigation path. All other requested facts (gross rents, company debt, trace of the $1,500,000 proceeds, distributions, how Bram himself was notified, and her sell-or-hold objective) draw **no additional information**; they are flagged as discovery/verification unknowns in `QUESTIONS.md` rather than re-asked.
74: 
75: ## 8. Risks, stated plainly
76: 
77: 1. **Actual notice / no-prejudice argument (former risks 1–2 merged; facts updated 2026-10).** The client saw the 2026-08-20 texted PDF with the full 30-day window and did not act; her email on file has been dead since 2019 and she never updated it. Defendants will argue (a) actual notice cured any delivery defect — no prejudice, since she could not have funded $270,000 in any event — and (b) her own stale address contributed to the email prong's failure. What we keep: the certified-mail prong failed **objectively and undisputedly** (never attempted, on the Manager's own production); the library states the rule is **strict compliance**; §6.3's "certified mail and email" is mandatory on its face. What we do not do: stake the case on delivery mechanics — the arithmetic ground leads and Count 1 is pleaded accordingly. Open fact: whether the full OA (the excerpts are partial) imposes any member duty to keep contact information current.
78: 2. **Tolling on the fee claims — strengthened by the client's 2026-10 answers; residual risks stated.** Pre-2023-10-08 fees ($375,000: 2022 + 2023 payments, both made before the 3-year cutoff) are presumptively barred; recovery depends on concealment tolling per the library. **Strengthened:** until 2026 the client received only one-page summaries carrying a generic "management expenses" line — the payee (the Manager's wholly-owned affiliate) was masked in the documents she was given; the affiliate identity and payment stream surfaced only in 2026 when her books-and-records demand produced bank statements. Masked counterparty + formal-demand diligence support inherent-unknowability, and the breached §5.4 30-day-disclosure duty supplies the affirmative basis for tolling. **Residual risks:** (i) the exact 2026 demand/response dates are unknown and set the limitations start point for the older payments; (ii) a court may still ask why she never inquired earlier into the "management expenses" line — the masked counterparty is the answer, but acknowledge the question; (iii) **QUANTUM remains unproven**: nothing in the file shows whether 6% of rents + $180–240k/yr is above or below market, no market benchmark exists anywhere in the library or the file, and the CSV shows the fees tracked the self-set schedule (180→195→210→225→240, i.e. +8.33%, +7.69%, +7.14%, +6.67% per year — no visible mischarging under the schedule itself). The fee claim's leverage is real; its dollar value is unproven.
79: 3. **Valuation risk cuts both ways.** A formal appraisal could come in below the broker's $9.8M (or above it). The broker's $14.5M/$9.8M is an opinion, not an appraisal; book ($3.1M) vs. market ($9.8M) is a 3.16× gap that needs to be explained by appreciated real estate, and confirmation of any company debt is needed (a remaining unknown — the client offers no further information; see QUESTIONS.md).
80: 4. **Cash burn.** Contingent-fee representation is the only realistic structure given her cash constraints. **[unverified]** Contingency percentages and Chancery cost expectations are market facts, not library facts — confirm with counsel.
81: 5. **Bram-objective risk.** He may use the Company's funds to defend and to buy more value-laden assets; if the dilution is rescinded, his $270,000 "payment" for her share returns to him (treat as loan to the Company or refund; structure in the prayer for relief).
82: 6. **Where the fee recovery lands.** Derivative recovery goes to the Company. If she is a member at settlement/close, her pro-rata benefit is ~18%. If she is bought out before that recovery materializes, she loses it — so any settlement should be struck **after** (or simultaneously with) resolution of the fee claim, or price it in.
83: 
84: ## 9. Open items — see `QUESTIONS.md`
85: 
86: The first two original open items are **closed** by the client's 2026-10 answers (notice facts; what she saw before 2026). Remaining unknowns — the client has no additional information, so these fall to discovery/verification, not re-asking:
87: 
88: 1. **Full operating agreement text** — the excerpts are partial; unknown provisions (member contact-information duty, indemnification, transfer restrictions, definitions) could affect the email prong and buyout mechanics. Obtain the full document.
89: 2. **Gross rents 2022–2026** — sizes the 6%-of-gross-rents property-management fee stream (quantum).
90: 3. **Company debt** — needed to explain the book ($3.1M) vs. broker ($9.8M) equity gap and to confirm the broker's $14.5M EV → $9.8M equity step.
91: 4. **Trace of the $1,500,000** since 2026-09-20 — bona fide purpose / pretext ground (§6.3 requires the stated purpose be bona fide and set forth in the notice).
92: 5. **Exact 2026 books-and-records demand/response dates** — sets the likely limitations start point for the pre-2023-10-08 fee payments under concealment tolling.
93: 6. **Market benchmark for the Castellan Asset Services fee** — arm's-length prong of §5.4; nothing in the library or the file supplies one.
94: 7. **Certified-mail history to Bram, distribution history 2022–2026, and the client's sell-or-hold objective** — leverage and settlement-shaping facts.
95: 
96: ## 10. Advice on the client's instruction to plead a fiduciary count anyway (2026-10)
97: 
98: **Exchange.** The client asked why, given the Manager's self-dealing, no fiduciary-duty count is pleaded — "every article I read says managers owe loyalty" — and asked to plead it anyway "to scare him."
99: 
100: **The law, stated plainly.** Her reading is correct *as the default rule*, but §7.3 is the parties' contractual switch-off of that default, and §18-1101(c) makes the elimination enforceable (quoted verbatim in §1 and §2 above). The §7.3 proviso preserves the implied covenant, and §18-1101(e) makes bad-faith-covenant liability non-eliminable. Honest limits, per the library (*Nemec*/*Gerber*): the implied covenant is a **gap-filler** that cannot override express terms and is **not** a substitute for fiduciary duties — its real force here is *Dieckman*-style policing of contractually vested discretion (the §6.3 "good faith" fair-value determination and "bona fide purpose" call), which is exactly where this case attacks.
101: 
102: **Why the count backfires rather than scares.**
103: 1. It is dismissible on the face of the complaint (§7.3 + §18-1101(c)); one easy kill lets opposing counsel brand the whole complaint as overreach and recovers the initiative the invalid dilution took away.
104: 2. Credibility is the currency of this case — the arithmetic/rescission fight needs the court's trust; a knowingly-waived count spends it.
105: 3. Fee/sanction exposure for a knowingly-eliminated claim **[unverified — fee-shifting and sanctions standards are not in this library]**.
106: 4. Contingent-fee economics: dollars defend a dead count instead of the counts that can return $1,764,000 / $675,000–$1,050,000.
107: 
108: **What delivers the scare instead (already in the complaint).** The derivative fee-disgorgement count ($675,000 in-window; up to $1,050,000 with tolling; bank statements from his own production, benchmark discovery); the rescission/arithmetic counts stranding his $270,000 self-purchase and restoring 18% (±$1,764,000); and the self-dealing facts pleaded prominently in the fact allegations — the charge, under labels that survive his motions.
109: 
110: **Disposition.** Recommendation stands: do not plead a fiduciary count. Client sign-off requested; if she instructs otherwise, record the disagreement in writing before filing (professional-responsibility handling **[unverified — conduct rules are outside this library]**), and re-contact the client on the dismissal risk to the whole complaint's optics.
